# Exact local depth after independently truncating simplex vertices

This is an ordinary convex-body theorem, not a resolution of OC. It gives
an exact all-direction calculation of a shape perturbation of every
simplex, including its maximizing point and its second-order coefficient.
No conclusion about a general mixed-integer source is inferred.

## 1. Statement and conventions

Let T be a d-dimensional simplex, d>=1, with vertices v_0,...,v_d,
barycentric coordinates lambda_0,...,lambda_d, and volume V. Write
m=d+1 and G=(d/m)^d. For small epsilon_i>=0 remove the open vertex
corners lambda_i>1-epsilon_i, and put

    K={x in T: lambda_i(x)<=1-epsilon_i for every i},
    t_i=epsilon_i^d,  t=sum_i t_i.

There is a dimension-only epsilon_*>0 such that, when all
epsilon_i<=epsilon_* and t>0, the following statements hold. The corners
have disjoint interiors and |K|=(1-t)V. There is a unique scalar D near G
satisfying

    prod_i(D+t_i) [sum_i 1/(D+t_i)]^d=d^d.             (1)

All denominators are positive. Put

    c=[sum_i 1/(D+t_i)]^{-1},
    lambda_i^*=c/(D+t_i).                             (2)

The point y_* with these barycentrics belongs to int K and is the unique
maximizer of ordinary absolute halfspace depth on K. Its absolute depth
is DV, and its normalized depth is D/(1-t). Every closed ambient
halfspace containing y_* has at least DV volume in K.

Smallness here is uniform over the vector of relative truncation sizes.
It is not a hypothesis about arbitrary convex perturbations of T. All
assertions are invariant under an invertible affine transformation of
the continuous space, so one fixed standard simplex suffices.

For d=1 the assertion in fact holds whenever epsilon_0+epsilon_1<1:
K is an interval and D=(1-t)/2, with y_* its midpoint.

## 2. The exact local vertex-cap formula for an untruncated simplex

Let g be the simplex centroid. There is a neighborhood U of g such that
the minimum volume of a halfspace through y in U is attained among
cuts that isolate exactly one vertex. For the cuts isolating vertex i,
the exact minimum, divided by V, is

    d^d prod_{j!=i} lambda_j(y).                      (3)

Here and below a containing halfspace can first be tightened parallel to
itself until its boundary passes through y, so through-point cuts suffice.

To prove the locality assertion, normalize continuous normals to the
unit sphere. The volume of T intersected with the through-y halfspace
is jointly continuous in y and the normal: convergent indicators agree
off their limiting hyperplane, which has d-dimensional volume zero, and
bounded convergence applies. At g its minimum is G V. The equality
case of the classical simplex Grunbaum inequality consists precisely of
the m apex-side, facet-parallel normals (for d=1 these are the two
directions). This equality classification is proved in the archived
continuous-minimum-maximal-depth-simplex-rigidity.md.

Choose small disjoint neighborhoods of those normals. At g, all normals
outside them have volume at least (G+eta)V for some eta>0, by continuity
on a compact set. Uniform continuity keeps this strict gap for y close
to g. In the neighborhood associated with i, the cut has vertex i
strictly on its included side and all other vertices strictly on the
excluded side. These strict signs hold uniformly after shrinking the
neighborhood and U. Thus every relevant cap is a simplex at vertex i.

In the non-i barycentrics such a cap has the form

    sum_{j!=i} a_j lambda_j(x)<=1,
    a_j>1,  sum_{j!=i} a_j lambda_j(y)=1.

Its volume fraction is prod_{j!=i} a_j^{-1}. AM-GM applied to the d
positive numbers a_j lambda_j(y), whose sum is one, makes this at least
(3). Equality holds for a_j=1/[d lambda_j(y)]. For y sufficiently close
to g, each d lambda_j(y)<1 and this optimal cap is in the chosen
neighborhood of the original canonical normal. This proves both
attainment and the exact value (3), with a unique optimal vertex-i
normal.

## 3. Uniform localization for the truncated bodies

Assume all epsilon_i are small enough that epsilon_i+epsilon_j<1 for
i!=j. The corner interiors are disjoint because otherwise
lambda_i+lambda_j>2-epsilon_i-epsilon_j>1. Each corner is a homothetic
simplex of volume t_i V, proving |K|=(1-t)V.

Halfspace depth on a compact set has a maximizer. Indeed it is upper
semicontinuous in the point: for a fixed normal, the through-point cap
volume is continuous here, and an infimum of continuous functions is
upper semicontinuous. The domain K is compact.

The point g belongs to K for small epsilon_i. Its absolute depth is at
least (G-t)V, since deletion removes at most tV from any cap. If y is
any maximum-depth point of K, each canonical cap
{lambda_i(x)>=lambda_i(y)} therefore gives

    G-t <= (1-lambda_i(y))^d,
    lambda_i(y)<=1-(G-t)^{1/d}.                      (4)

The right side tends to 1/m. Since the barycentrics sum to one, all of
them tend uniformly to 1/m. Consequently every maximizer is in U when
t is sufficiently small. This localizes ALL maximizing points, without
assuming a priori that one of them is on a symmetry axis.

For y in a fixed sufficiently small U, the canonical normal gaps from
Section 2 remain uniform. Removing the corners changes every cap by at
most tV, so the minimum for K also lies in the union of the chosen
normal neighborhoods when t is small. In the i-th neighborhood the
entire i-th deleted corner lies strictly inside the cap and all other
deleted corners lie strictly outside it. This follows uniformly from
the strict included/excluded vertex signs: each corner has diameter
O(epsilon_i), and the normals and y vary in compact sufficiently small
neighborhoods. Equivalently, the coefficients a_j above are uniformly
bounded and bounded away from one, so on the i-corner their sum is at
most (max a_j)epsilon_i<1; on any other corner it remains >1.

Thus the exact depth at EVERY y in U is

    depth_abs,K(y)/V
       = min_i {d^d prod_{j!=i}lambda_j(y)-t_i}.     (5)

The minimizing one-vertex normal in (3) lies in the same neighborhood,
so subtracting t_i does not change its optimization. There is no
uncontrolled direction or partial-deletion term in (5).

## 4. Existence of the scalar solution and its global local optimum

For positive D near G define

    F(D,t_0,...,t_d)
      =prod_i(D+t_i)[sum_i 1/(D+t_i)]^d-d^d.

At t_i=0 this is m^d D-d^d. Its derivative with respect to D at
(G,0,...,0) is m^d>0. By continuity the derivative stays positive in
a small fixed neighborhood. Fix a smaller interval about G. Its endpoint
values have opposite signs when all t_i are small; the intermediate
value theorem and strict monotonicity give a unique root there. It
tends uniformly to G as max_i t_i tends to zero. This elementary
argument also supplies smooth dependence by implicit differentiation,
or by the usual one-variable inverse function theorem.

Definitions (1)-(2) give sum_i lambda_i^*=1. Furthermore

    d^d prod_i lambda_i^*=c,
    d^d prod_{j!=i}lambda_j^* - t_i=D.               (6)

The first identity follows by substituting (1) into the product in (2).
All lambda_i^* tend to 1/m, so y_* is in U and int K, and

    w_i=1-d lambda_i^*>0,   sum_i w_i=1.             (7)

These positive weights prove that (6) is the UNIQUE maximum of the
local expression (5), not merely a stationary point. Suppose lambda
has positive coordinates summing to one and every expression in (5)
is at least D. Put r_j=lambda_j/lambda_j^*. By (6),

    prod_{j!=i} r_j>=1  for every i.

Multiply their logarithms by w_i and sum. Because 1-w_j=d lambda_j^*,

    0 <= sum_i w_i sum_{j!=i} log r_j
       =d sum_j lambda_j^* log r_j
       <=d log(sum_j lambda_j^* r_j)=0.             (8)

The last inequality is the strict concavity of log, whose equality
condition forces all r_j equal. Their weighted sum is one, so every
r_j=1. Hence lambda=lambda^*. If any local point other than y_* had
depth at least D, (8) would contradict its being distinct. Section 3
puts every global maximizer in U, while (5)-(6) show y_* has depth D.
This proves the theorem, including uniqueness and all halfspaces.

## 5. Exact one-corner formula and planar closed form

For a single corner t_0=t and t_i=0 for i>=1, (2) makes
lambda_1^*=...=lambda_d^*=b and lambda_0^*=1-db. The equation becomes

    d^d b^{d-1}((d+1)b-1)=t,
    D=d^d(1-db)b^{d-1},                              (9)

where b is the unique root near 1/(d+1). For d=2,

    b=(1+sqrt(1+3t))/6,
    D=2(1+sqrt(1+3t))/9-2t/3.                       (10)

The optimal caps at vertices i>=1 are generally OBLIQUE to the
opposite original facets. Replacing their true value by
(1-b)^d would give the correct first-order term but an incorrect
exact formula and second-order term.

## 6. First and second variations with exact constants

Set t_i=s tau_i for a fixed nonnegative vector tau, and write
T_1=sum_i tau_i, tau_bar=T_1/m, b_i=tau_i-tau_bar. Expanding the
logarithm of (1), or differentiating it twice, gives

    D(s)=G-s T_1/m
         -s^2 (d-1)/(2mG) sum_i b_i^2+O(s^3),       (11)

    lambda_i^*(s)=1/m
         +s(tau_bar-tau_i)/(mG)+O(s^2).             (12)

For completeness, writing D=G-s tau_bar+s^2 B+O(s^3) yields
sum log(D+s tau_i)+d log(sum 1/(D+s tau_i)) equal to its constant
term plus

    s^2[B/G+(d-1)/(2mG^2)sum_i b_i^2]+O(s^3).

Its vanishing proves the quadratic coefficient in (11). The normalized
depth is therefore

    G+s(G-1/m)T_1
      +s^2[(G-1/m)T_1^2
            -(d-1)/(2mG)sum_i b_i^2]+O(s^3).        (13)

For d>=2 and nonzero tau, G>1/m, so the first normalized variation
is strictly positive. If all corners have equal relative volume,
lambda_i^*=1/m and D=G-t/m EXACTLY throughout this small regime.
These formulas concern an ordinary convex body of dimension d and
track normalization by its remaining volume; they do not establish
a mixed-integer allocation inequality.

## 7. Boundary and verification scope

All measures here are full d-dimensional Lebesgue measure, equal to
the standard H_d on the affine span. For small truncations K is a
convex body, all cap boundaries have zero such measure, and closed
inequalities are retained throughout. Zero individual t_i cause no
singularity in (1)-(13); the all-zero vector gives the original
simplex and its unique centroid maximum. Dimension one was separately
settled in Section 1. No unproved interchange of optimizing points
and limits is used: (4) localizes every optimizer before (5) is applied.

The accompanying exact verifier checks the defining algebra, planar
closed form, and the first and second implicit derivatives. The
all-direction reduction and maximizing certificate (8) are analytic
proofs, not consequences of finite numerical normal screens.
